wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e111.summary: Poses a further question annexed to the third principal question: whether God under the proper ratio of deity is the subject of theology. Two arguments for no. (1) The first subject is what all the science's properties belong to first, but many theological properties belong first to creatures (the rational soul's beatification, the future resurrection) or to the persons (the Father generates). (2) Every subject of a science can be known both indistinctly (presupposed) and distinctly (acquired), but God cannot, because a simple thing is known either wholly or not at all (Metaphysics VII), and God is infinitely simple.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e146.summary: Third argument: God is the subject of a naturally acquired science, since metaphysics proves many properties of God, and the same thing under the same ratio is not the subject of different sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e157.summary: Confirmation: what is proved in a lower science cannot be the subject of a higher one, since the subject is simply first in its science. God's existence is proved in natural science and metaphysics, so God cannot be theology's subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e168.summary: Argument to the contrary: the noblest habit has the noblest subject under the noblest ratio, and theology is the noblest habit.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e178.summary: Identifies the preliminary difficulty, what belongs to the ratio of a science's first subject, and plans to treat it first and then the question.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e185.summary: Reports an opinion (Scotus's): the ratio of a first subject is to contain virtually and first all the truths of the habit. First proof: the first subject contains the immediate propositions, since their subject contains the predicate and so the evidence of the whole proposition, and immediate propositions contain the conclusions.
claims: The first subject virtually contains all the truths of its science (reported).
The subject of an immediate proposition contains its predicate (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e203.summary: Second proof: primacy is taken in Posterior Analytics I from the definition of the universal as adequation. The object relates to the habit as cause to effect, and a cause is adequate only if it virtually contains the whole effect.
claims: The object relates to the habit as cause to effect (reported).
An adequate cause virtually contains the whole effect (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e223.summary: The opinion explains 'first virtually': the first does not depend on another, while others depend on it. So to contain virtually is not to depend on others in containing but to have others depend on it: with everything else impossibly removed and the intellect remaining, it would still contain, and nothing else contains except through its ratio.
claims: Virtual containment as first means containing independently of anything else (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e239.summary: Another explanation by the opinion: in essentially ordered things one must stop at a simply first. The knowables of a science are essentially ordered: conclusions are known from principles, immediate principles from their terms, and the predicate's term from the subject's ratio (principles being second-mode per se, the subject falls in the predicate's definition, Metaphysics VII). So one reaches a simple subject of the principle, from whose knowledge everything in the science is known and which is known from nothing else.
claims: The knowables of a science are essentially ordered (reported).
Second-mode principles include the subject in the predicate's definition (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e268.summary: Ockham argues against the opinion, first that it does not belong to a subject to contain virtually the knowledge of its property, and second that it does not belong to it to contain virtually the property itself. On the first: an efficient cause contains its effect no less perfectly than a subject its property, and the efficient or final cause is the most perfect containment of something really distinct (material containment is weaker, and only efficient containment fits God). Yet knowledge of a cause does not virtually contain knowledge of its effect, since on the opponent's view distinct quiddities require distinct rationes cognoscendi. So knowledge of a subject would not contain knowledge of its property.
claims: An efficient cause contains its effect at least as perfectly as a subject its property.
Knowledge of a cause does not virtually contain knowledge of its effect.
Distinct quiddities require distinct rationes cognoscendi (the opponent's principle).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e315.summary: Possible reply: distinct rationes cognoscendi are required for distinct quiddities only when one does not virtually contain the other.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e322.summary: Counter: then a distinct ratio of the sun would suffice for distinctly knowing all lower quiddities, since the sun virtually contains them all.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e331.summary: Possible reply: it does not suffice, because the sun is not the total cause of lower things.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e338.summary: Counter: then another cause is required for distinctly knowing the effect. Since a subject is likewise not always the total cause of its property, distinct knowledge of the subject does not suffice for distinct knowledge of the property.
claims: A subject is not always the total cause of its property.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e349.summary: Another reply: a property has more and more intimate dependences on its subject than an effect has on its cause, so knowledge of the subject suffices where knowledge of a cause does not.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e365.summary: Counter: sometimes a property depends on its subject only as an accident, and that dependence is less perfect than an effect's dependence on its efficient cause.
claims: Accidental dependence is weaker than dependence on an efficient cause.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e375.summary: Further, from the doctor's own Reportatio Parisiensis: when several items are each attained by a power or habit through its own formal ratio, none is first object by primacy of virtue, so knowledge of one does not contain knowledge of another. Subject and property are often distinct things on his view, since he proves that the subject efficiently causes its property. Every absolute thing distinct by its formal ratio moves the intellect, since every item contained under a power's adequate object (being) moves it. Confirmation: what moves sense can move the intellect, and an accident moves sense by its own power. Also, an absolute accident could exist without its subject and be seen intuitively without any knowledge of the subject. So a property moves the intellect per se, and knowledge of one does not contain knowledge of the other.
claims: If each item is attained through its own formal ratio, none is first by primacy of virtue.
Every absolute thing can by itself move the intellect, since being is its adequate object.
An absolute accident could exist and be intuited without its subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e425.summary: Confirmation from Posterior Analytics I: lacking a sense, one lacks the science that depends on it. The objects of one sense sometimes cause the objects of another (tangible qualities causing colors and tastes, on many views and seemingly Aristotle's). So however perfectly one knew tangibles, without sight one could not know colors. Knowledge of a cause does not virtually contain knowledge of its effect, and likewise, if tangible qualities were subjects of the others, knowledge of the subject would not suffice to know the property.
claims: Lacking a sense, one lacks the knowledge dependent on it.
Perfect knowledge of tangible qualities would not yield knowledge of colors without sight.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e456.summary: Second argument: on the opponent's principles, what contains perfect knowledge of something contains its imperfect knowledge. But knowledge of a subject does not contain even the most imperfect knowledge of its property, its quid nominis, which must be known beforehand. So the subject virtually contains no knowledge of the property.
claims: Knowledge of a subject does not contain even the nominal definition of its property.
The quid nominis of a property must be known beforehand.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e472.summary: Third argument: virtual containment of knowledge of a conclusion belongs most to the middle term (middle and cause are the same, Posterior Analytics II), and the subject is not the middle. Also, one can distinctly know the subject yet not know that the property belongs to it because its extrinsic cause is unknown: one can abstractively know the moon without knowing whether it is eclipsed, not knowing whether the earth interposes.
claims: Virtual containment of a conclusion belongs most to the middle term.
One can know the subject distinctly without knowing its property, for lack of knowing its extrinsic cause.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e496.summary: Possible reply: the middle is the subject's definition and so really the subject, so containment attributed to the middle belongs to the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e512.summary: Counter: on their view the middle is the cause of the property's inherence, which is often an extrinsic cause really distinct from the subject (as in the eclipse example), so virtual containment belongs to something other than the subject.
claims: The cause of a property's inherence is often extrinsic to the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e524.summary: Confirmation: according to Aristotle (Physics I, Posterior Analytics), knowledge of a thing depends on knowledge of all its causes (to be explained later). So knowledge of a property depends on knowledge of other causes too, and the subject does not first contain the property.
claims: Knowledge of a thing depends on knowledge of all its causes.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e540.summary: Fourth argument: on this doctor's view nothing leads to knowledge of another unless it contains it virtually or essentially. Many properties are respective or connotative and can only be known after knowing something not contained in the subject. 'Beatifiable' is a property of the rational creature but cannot be known without knowing beatitude, since the term of a relation must be known first. Similarly 'creatable', 'able to have charity', and matter's 'informable'. Form, charity and beatitude are not contained in those subjects virtually or essentially, so knowledge of the subject does not cause knowledge of these properties.
claims: Respective and connotative properties can only be known after knowing their terms.
The terms of such properties (beatitude, charity, form) are not contained in their subjects.
Knowledge of a relation depends on knowledge of its term.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e595.summary: Answers the objection that these are not properties properly speaking, since a subject is more perfect than its property and causes it efficiently. These propositions, being necessary, must be per se in the first or second mode. They are not first-mode, so they are second-mode, and the predicate is a property, though not always a proper one. Whether or not the property is more perfect, something it imports can be more perfect than the subject, and knowledge of the less perfect does not contain knowledge of the more perfect. That the subject efficiently causes its property will be shown false later.
claims: Necessary propositions are per se in the first or second mode.
Something imported by a property can be more perfect than the subject.
Knowledge of the less perfect does not contain knowledge of the more perfect.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e634.summary: Another reply: it suffices to know what the property imports under a concept common to it and other things, and the first subject virtually contains such confused knowledge, and so knowledge of the property.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e650.summary: Counter: these properties import something not only in general but in particular, such as 'creatable by three supposits subsisting in one nature', and such properties can never be known by virtue of the subject.
claims: Some properties import particular terms (e.g., the three divine persons) not knowable from the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e661.summary: Fifth argument: if the subject so contained the predicate, then once a subject was known any property could be evidently known of it, through the property's knowledge, the premises, and the conclusion. That is false: 'the intellective soul is beatifiable', 'man can see the divine essence', 'man can have charity' cannot be known naturally, only supernaturally.
claims: If subjects virtually contained properties, any property would be evidently knowable once the subject was known.
That the soul is beatifiable cannot be known naturally.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e688.summary: The doctor's reply: the soul or intellective power is not naturally knowable to us under the proper, special ratio by which it is ordered to such an end and capable of confirming grace. In this state we know the soul and our nature only under a general ratio abstracted from sensibles, under which it is not ordered to beatitude or vision. So these properties cannot be known from the knowledge of the subject possible to us in this state.
claims: In this state we know the soul only under a general ratio abstracted from sensibles (Scotus, reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e712.summary: Counter: our soul under that ratio is naturally knowable by itself or by another intellectual nature, yet that end is naturally knowable by no intellectual nature. Also, 'perpetuable to infinity' is a property of lower things, yet cannot be evidently known however distinctly the subjects are known.
claims: Our supernatural end is naturally knowable by no intellect.
Some properties of distinctly known things remain unknowable.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e728.summary: Further: on his view accidents are distinctly known by us in this state, yet their dependence on substance cannot be known in particular, as neither can the substance. And however distinctly accidents are known, not all their causes can be known in particular. So many properties of creatures cannot be known naturally however well their subjects are known.
claims: Accidents are known distinctly in this life but their dependence on substance is not known in particular.
Many properties of creatures are naturally unknowable however well their subjects are known.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e750.summary: Sixth argument: then every property of being would be self-evident of being. If the subject so contains the predicate, every proposition stating a property of being would be known from its terms, because being can only be known distinctly, being simply simple. Take any such proposition: if known from its terms, the point is granted. If not, distinct knowledge of the subject does not first contain knowledge of the property, and something else is required.
claims: On the opponent's view every property of being would be self-evident of being.
Being is simply simple and can only be known distinctly (opponent's view).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e779.summary: Possible reply: one prior property is virtually contained in being and contains a later property, so the later cannot be known from being without it.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e795.summary: Counter from his own exposition: the first contains virtually with everything else impossibly removed, so with the prior property removed it would still contain the later one.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e805.summary: Further: it would follow that we in this state could evidently know all properties of being, since knowing being (which can only be distinct) yields the first property, then the second, and so on. That is false: we cannot evidently know that every being is intuitively knowable by us, as even this doctor holds. Then the reply is raised that the opinion means not that incomplex knowledge of the subject causes incomplex knowledge of the property, but complex knowledge.
claims: We cannot evidently know all properties of being in this life.
We cannot evidently know that every being is intuitively knowable by us.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e834.summary: Counter: that does not seem to be his intent. His first argument says propositions are contained in terms and the predicate term in the subject, so he means incomplex knowledge containing incomplex knowledge. His exposition of 'first containing', as containing independently, can only hold if the subject contains incomplex knowledge of the property.
claims: Scotus's theory concerns incomplex knowledge containing incomplex knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e860.summary: Further, his second argument takes the subject as the adequate cause of the whole habit, and so of the incomplex knowledge of the property.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e867.summary: Similarly, his argument from essential order implies that incomplex cognitions are essentially ordered with a first containing the others. His example that the isosceles contains all the triangle's properties means the triangle, an incomplex, virtually contains its properties.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e885.summary: Further, he often assumes that any object, with the agent or possible intellect cooperating to the limit of its power, produces as adequate effect its own proper concept and the concept of everything essentially or virtually included in it. Only complex inclusions require discourse, and he says that virtually included items are not known from the subject by discourse. He holds that beyond its proper concept and what it includes, nothing is known from the subject except by discourse, which presupposes simple cognition. So he means incomplex knowledge.
claims: Scotus holds that an object produces its own concept and those of what it virtually includes.
Discourse presupposes simple cognition.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e922.summary: Further, he takes the proposition that no subject produces its own proper simple concept and that of another object unless it contains that object essentially or virtually, so the subject causes the simple concept of what it virtually includes. Ockham then argues his second point, that the subject does not always virtually include its property. This could only be by causing a really distinct inhering thing or by causing the concept of the thing. Not the latter, since causing a concept means causing knowledge, which has been refuted. Not the former, since many properties ('creative', 'true', 'good') are not things really distinct from their subjects on their view.
claims: A subject does not always virtually include its property.
Properties like 'creative', 'true', 'good' are not really distinct from their subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e969.summary: Further: sometimes a property imports something more perfect than the subject, as 'in potency to form' imports form, which is more perfect than matter. The more perfect is not contained in the less perfect, or knowledge of the less perfect would contain knowledge of the more perfect, against them.
claims: Form is more perfect than matter.
The more perfect is not virtually contained in the less perfect.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e982.summary: Ockham's first thesis on this article: knowledge of one extramental incomplex thing is never, even with the intellect, a sufficient cause of the first incomplex knowledge of another thing.
claims: Incomplex knowledge of one thing never suffices to cause the first incomplex knowledge of another.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e993.summary: Second thesis: a subject does not always virtually contain its property.
claims: A subject does not always virtually contain its property.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e998.summary: Third thesis: distinct incomplex knowledge of the subject and of the property does not always suffice for knowledge of the proposition composed of them.
claims: Distinct incomplex knowledge of subject and property does not always suffice for knowledge of the proposition.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1007.summary: Fourth thesis announced: Ockham will show what belongs to the ratio of a first subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1012.summary: Proves the first thesis from experience. However intuitively and perfectly one knows something, one never thereby knows another thing unless one already has knowledge of it. Someone who knew lower things but never saw the heavenly bodies would have no knowledge of sun, moon or stars. The reason: all abstractive knowledge of a thing, or proper simple knowledge of it, naturally presupposes intuitive knowledge of that same thing, and intuitive knowledge can naturally be caused only by the thing itself, mediately or immediately (God could do otherwise). Even between cause and effect, the most essential order, incomplex knowledge of one does not contain that of the other. One who intuitively saw a substance would not thereby distinctly know any particular accident. Objection: if the subject were known in its whole being, including as subject of this property, the property would be known, and likewise a cause known as cause would make the effect known.
claims: Incomplex knowledge of one thing never yields knowledge of another not previously apprehended.
Abstractive or proper simple knowledge of a thing presupposes intuitive knowledge of that thing.
Intuitive knowledge of a thing can naturally be caused only by the thing itself.
Intuitive knowledge of substance does not yield distinct knowledge of its accidents.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1085.summary: Answers the first part of the objection. The 'rationes' or modes of being under which the subject would be known either signify something in reality or nothing. If nothing, the subject can be known distinctly and perfectly without them. If something, they signify the thing's quiddity (which can be known without any property), part of it, or something accidental. In the last case these rationes are themselves properties, so the objection amounts to saying that if the subject were known along with its properties, its properties would be known.
claims: The whole quiddity of a thing can be known without knowledge of any property.
Knowing a subject 'in all its rationes' just means knowing it with its properties.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1111.summary: Further: knowing something as subject of a property presupposes knowledge of the property, so that knowledge is an effect rather than a cause of knowing the property.
claims: Knowing something as subject of a property presupposes knowing the property.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1122.summary: Consequence: the same subject under the same ratio, on the subject's side, can be subject of diverse properties, as of diverse accidents, though the accidents give rise to different denominations, which are properties rather than subjects. 'Heatable' and 'coolable' presuppose no distinction in the subject. Being necessarily predicated of it, they are second-mode per se and so are properties. The same holds of 'mobile' and 'quantified' with respect to substance. These are the rationes that lead many to posit distinct sciences of the same subject under different rationes, natural science of body as mobile and mathematics of body as quantified, though these rationes are really properties of body.
claims: One subject under the same ratio can be subject of diverse properties.
'Heatable' and 'coolable' presuppose no distinction in the subject.
'Mobile' and 'quantified' are properties of body, not distinct rationes of the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1172.summary: It follows that distinct sciences of the same subject can arise from the distinction of properties alone, without any distinction on the subject's side. A science thus depends equally on property and subject and is in its way virtually contained in the property as in the subject, so the subject does not first contain the science, since it depends on the property in containing.
claims: Distinct sciences of one subject can arise solely from distinct properties.
A science depends equally on property and subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1188.summary: Answers the second part of the objection: knowing a cause as cause presupposes knowing the effect, since 'cause as cause' signifies a relation and a relation presupposes knowledge of both foundation and term. So it is not the cause of knowing the effect but the reverse.
claims: Knowing a cause as cause presupposes knowledge of the effect.
Knowledge of a relation presupposes knowledge of foundation and term.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1201.summary: Further: just as one who knows a cause as cause knows the effect, one who knows an effect as effect knows the cause, so knowledge of the cause contains knowledge of the effect no more than the reverse.
claims: Knowledge of cause as cause and of effect as effect are symmetrical.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1213.summary: Further: every thing has such rationes relative to all things, since it exceeds or is exceeded by each in perfection. So it could not be known under all such rationes without knowing everything, and every thing would virtually contain knowledge of all things.
claims: Every thing stands in relations of perfection to all others.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1233.summary: Reports a reply by some: knowledge of a property can be virtually contained in something in three ways: as in an efficient cause, as in a representing object, or as in a subject immediately containing a property necessarily predicated of it. Only the third pertains necessarily to the science of that subject.
claims: Virtual containment of property-knowledge can be causal, representational, or subjective (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1253.summary: Ockham replies that this is beside the point: then 'the subject virtually contains knowledge of the property' just means 'the subject virtually contains the property', but a subject can contain the property without being able to cause knowledge of it.
claims: Containing a property is distinct from causing knowledge of it.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1264.summary: Proves the second thesis: a subject does not always virtually contain its property, since properties are often respective concepts (on some views) or connotative ones (on others) and import things not virtually contained in the subject.
claims: Respective or connotative properties import things not contained in the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1277.summary: Proves the third thesis: distinct knowledge of subject and property does not always contain knowledge of the immediate proposition. On this doctor's view 'heat is calefactive' is immediate, with no cause sought beyond heat being heat. Yet someone who intuitively saw heat and distinctly knew that the sun warms lower things, but never experienced heat producing heat (no heatable thing being nearby), would no more evidently know that heat is calefactive than that whiteness produces whiteness.
claims: Distinct knowledge of subject and property does not suffice for knowledge of an immediate proposition.
That heat is calefactive is known only through experience.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1314.summary: So knowledge of such truths often requires intuitive knowledge, through which evident knowledge of a contingent proposition is had, without which evident knowledge of the universal and necessary one cannot be had, as explained above.
claims: Evident knowledge of universal necessary truths often requires intuitive knowledge of contingent ones.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1326.summary: The same holds for man and risibility: if someone never experienced a man laughing, they would not know whether man is risible.
claims: Man's risibility is known only through experience.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1335.summary: Fourth thesis: what does not belong to the ratio of a subject. Not virtual containment of its properties. Not that the science is named or specified by it, since one subject, the same in reality and ratio, can have distinct sciences through distinct properties. Not that the science gets its dignity from it, since with the same subject one science can be nobler through a nobler property ('every man is beatifiable' versus 'risible', 'the soul is beatifiable' versus 'peccable'). Not that it is the first thing the intellect meets in the science, since properties are sometimes prior in generation or perfection (accidents and acts are better known than subjects; form, imported by matter's property, is more perfect than matter). So the subject need not be the first mover of the intellect. Nor is knowledge of the subject the principal aim, since the aim is knowledge of the whole proposition. Sometimes the subject is known equally well beforehand: the moon is no better known by knowing it is eclipsed, but something else about it is learned.
claims: It does not belong to a subject to specify its science.
A science's dignity can come from its property rather than its subject.
Properties are sometimes better known or more perfect than their subjects.
The principal aim of a science is knowledge of the whole proposition.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1416.summary: Positive account: all that belongs to the ratio of a science's subject is that it is the subject of the predicate in a proposition known by scientia proprie dicta. Universally, the subject of the science and the subject of the known conclusion are the same under the same ratio. A science cannot be had without knowing its subject, but it can be had without knowing anything that is not a premise, the conclusion, the conclusion's subject or predicate, or the middle. So the subject of the science is the subject of the conclusion.
claims: The subject of a science is the subject of the known conclusion.
Being subject in a known proposition is all that belongs to the ratio of a science's subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1442.summary: Confirmation: every subject of a science is an incomplex. Apart from the conclusion's subject and predicate, the only incomplex is the middle, and the subject is neither the predicate nor the middle.
claims: Every subject of a science is an incomplex term.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1453.summary: Answers the objection that this concerns only a science of one conclusion by one demonstration, while the question concerns a science of many conclusions. As the subject of each partial science relates to that partial science, so the subject of the total science, if there is one, relates to the whole. So the subject of the whole science and of all its conclusions are simply the same.
claims: The subject of a total science is the common subject of all its conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1479.summary: Further: on their own view the subject is that of which properties are considered, and that is always the subject of the conclusion or conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1491.summary: Further: the first ratio of a subject is that which, posited with all else removed, makes something a subject, and without which nothing else suffices. Being the subject of a conclusion known by strict science alone, without virtual containment or other conditions, makes something truly a subject, since the science truly has a subject and only the conclusion's subject can be given.
claims: Being subject of a scientifically known conclusion is necessary and sufficient for being a science's subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1520.summary: Likewise, given any other condition, if something is not subject in the conclusion, it cannot be subject in the science.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1527.summary: Likewise, the ratio of the subject is either the conclusion's subject itself, in which case ratio and subject are simply the same, or a part of the subject. A science cannot be had without knowing the ratio of its subject, but it can be had without knowing anything that is not a complex or term (or term-part) in the demonstration. The ratio cannot be a complex, the middle or the predicate, so it is the subject or part of it.
claims: The ratio of the subject is the subject itself or part of it.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1549.summary: Confirmation: the ratio of the subject relates to science somewhat as the ratio cognoscendi relates to cognition. The ratio cognoscendi always concurs in cognition, so the ratio of the subject always concurs in science, and science cannot be had with it unknown or unexpressed.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1565.summary: Objection: in knowing 'every man is susceptible of learning', the ratio of the subject is the intellective soul, through which the property belongs to man, yet the soul is neither subject nor part of the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1576.summary: Reply: the ratio of the subject, as discussed here, is distinguished from both predicate and middle. Since the soul is that through which the property belongs to man, it is the middle of the demonstration, not the ratio of the subject.
claims: What explains why a property belongs to a subject is the middle term, not the ratio of the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1590.summary: Objections arise. First doubt: knowledge of the subject seems to contain knowledge of the property, because things are related in knowability as in being, and the subject causes the property's being.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1603.summary: Further, from Averroes (De anima I, Physics IV comm. 31): all properties and accidents are known through the subject's definition. A complete definition of place must resolve the questions about it and show the cause of all sensible accidents in it, since complete definitions give the cause of all accidents in the thing.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1623.summary: From this authority it seems that when something is known distinctly and by definition, every accident of it, and all the more every property, can be known through that knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1634.summary: Further: knowledge of principles virtually contains knowledge of conclusions, and knowledge of the inferior contains knowledge of the superior, so it is not unfitting for one knowledge to contain another.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1643.summary: Further: knowledge of a likeness, such as a statue, causes knowledge of what it is a likeness of.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1650.summary: Second doubt: knowledge of causes seems sufficient to cause knowledge of the effect, as Aristotle seems to hold in Physics I and elsewhere.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1664.summary: Third doubt: the subject of a science does not seem to be the same as the subject of the conclusion, since each science (metaphysics, natural philosophy) has one first subject but many conclusions with many subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1677.summary: Further: as object relates to power, so subject relates to science, and a power's first object is common to all its other objects, so a science's first subject is common to all others.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1686.summary: Further, Averroes on Metaphysics III: as medicine considers all things attributed to health, one science should consider all things attributed to being. So being seems to be the first subject of all conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1697.summary: Fourth doubt: what is the subject of a habit by which both principles and conclusion are known?

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1704.summary: Fifth doubt: how there can be distinct sciences of the same subject under the same ratio.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1711.summary: Answers the first objection: even if the subject virtually contained the property, knowledge of the subject would not contain knowledge of the property. The parallel between being and knowability holds for nobility (nobler being, nobler knowability), not for causality. Otherwise, since complex knowledge of an effect can cause complex knowledge of its cause, the effect would cause its cause. Also, the sun virtually causes a worm and heat, yet incomplex knowledge of the sun does not cause incomplex knowledge of them.
claims: The parallel between being and knowability holds for nobility, not causality.
Knowledge of an effect can cause knowledge of its cause, though the effect does not cause the cause.
Incomplex knowledge of the sun does not cause incomplex knowledge of its effects.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1749.summary: Answers the Averroes authority: a definition is the 'cause of all accidents' in that the subject's definition, or part of it, concurs as a partial cause in acquiring complex knowledge of the subject's properties and accidents. Sometimes one part demonstrates some properties and another part others.
claims: The subject's definition is a partial cause in acquiring complex knowledge of properties.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1767.summary: So through the rational soul as middle it is shown of man that he can discern, syllogize and sin, and through the body that he is risible and alterable. The cause of all accidents appears through the definition or its parts, but not without experience, so the definition is not the total cause. Alternatively, the Commentator speaks of a definition by addition, fitting place, which if complete expresses what distinguishes it and so helps resolve difficult questions without excluding other knowledge. To the next argument: one knowledge can contain another by inference (premises to conclusion), by composition (knowledge of terms yielding evident knowledge of a proposition), or by abstraction (knowledge of a singular yielding knowledge of a common concept, impossible without some singular). But knowledge of one singular is never, with the intellect, a sufficient cause of knowledge of another singular not common to it.
claims: Man's rational capacities are demonstrated through the soul and his bodily properties through the body.
The definition is not the total cause of knowledge of accidents; experience is required.
One knowledge can contain another by inference, composition, or abstraction.
Knowledge of one singular never suffices for knowledge of another singular.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1835.summary: Answers the argument from likeness: knowledge of a likeness causes knowledge of its original only with habitual knowledge of the original already present. Someone who saw a statue of Hercules with no prior knowledge of Hercules would think of Hercules no more than of Achilles. One who knew Hercules is led, by the habitual knowledge plus the sight, to an act of remembering, not to a first knowledge of him. So knowledge of one extramental thing does not lead, with the intellect, to the first incomplex knowledge of another thing in itself, meaning knowledge by which, in whole or part, nothing other than that thing is understood. This disposes of the objection that I know the pope whom I have never seen.
claims: A likeness causes knowledge of its original only given prior habitual knowledge of it.
Images cause recollection, not first knowledge.
Knowing a thing 'in itself' means a cognition in which nothing else is understood.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1874.summary: If asked for the cause of these claims, Ockham says it is the nature of things, made known to us by experience, since we experience all these things in ourselves.
claims: These epistemic facts are grounded in the nature of things and known by inner experience.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1883.summary: Answers the second doubt: knowledge of all causes together does not suffice to cause incomplex knowledge of the effect, though cognitions of the causes concur as partial causes of complex knowledge of the effect. Aristotle means discursive knowledge, which holds only between complexes.
claims: Knowledge of all causes does not suffice for incomplex knowledge of the effect.
Knowledge of causes is a partial cause of complex knowledge of the effect.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1899.summary: Answers the third doubt: strictly speaking, metaphysics and mathematics do not have one subject. There are as many subjects of sciences as subjects of conclusions. These subjects can stand in orders of predication (common and inferior), perfection, or totality (whole and part). The first among them is often called the first subject of the whole science, which is not strictly true, since the science is not one and has no single subject. In the Physics, natural body is first by predication relative to some, by perfection to others, and by totality to matter and form, but it is the subject only of the part demonstrating properties of natural body as such. That is why the same subject is assigned to the Physics and to all natural philosophy, and to the Prior Analytics (syllogism) and all logic, though other books have their own subjects. This may also explain why some made being the subject of metaphysics and others God: God is first in perfection and being first in predication.
claims: Strictly speaking, a science has as many subjects as its conclusions have.
Subjects in a science may be ordered by predication, perfection, or totality.
Natural body is the subject only of the part of physics dealing with natural body as such.
Being is first by predication and God first by perfection among metaphysical subjects.
concepts: being vs. God as subject of metaphysics

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e1998.summary: Develops this: as natural philosophy and mathematics are each one science only in an extended sense, with distinct parts having distinct subjects, so the books of the Physics, geometry and the like have parts with distinct subjects ordered as described. De anima has distinct subjects for its treatments of soul in general, the sensitive soul and the intellective soul. Soul, intellective soul and sensitive soul relate as superior and inferior just as body, celestial body and generable body do, which are accepted as subjects of distinct parts of natural philosophy. As the Categories (incomplexes), De interpretatione (complexes) and Prior Analytics (syllogism) have distinct subjects, so do the parts treating prime matter and the composite.
claims: Natural philosophy and mathematics are one science only in an extended sense.
Parts of the De anima treating different kinds of soul have distinct subjects.
Books of logic have distinct subjects according to their topics.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2074.summary: Answers the analogy with powers: a subject does not relate to a science as an object to a power. The object terminates the power's act, whereas the subject is not what is known and terminates the act of knowing only partially.
claims: The subject of a science only partially terminates the act of knowing.
The analogy between a power's object and a science's subject fails.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2085.summary: Answers Averroes: he takes 'one science' broadly and 'first subject' for what is first among all subjects in some way. In that sense being is the first subject of metaphysics, being first in predication, while the different parts still have different subjects. Strictly, the Commentator's statement is false, since being is not the subject of all parts of metaphysics. As he means it, though, 'being is the subject of metaphysics' means 'among all subjects of metaphysics's parts, being is first in predication'. Asking for the subject of metaphysics is like asking who is king of the whole world or all Christendom: different kingdoms have different kings, none is king of all, yet they may be ordered by power or wealth.
claims: Being is the first subject of metaphysics only in the sense of being first by predication.
Strictly, metaphysics has no single subject.
Subjects of a science are like kings of different kingdoms.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2140.summary: Answers the fourth doubt: a habit that is equivalently understanding of principles and science of the conclusion has the conclusion's subject as its subject, since the subject must be an incomplex other than the predicate or middle. If one habit could cover principles and conclusions with distinct subjects, it would have many subjects, those of all the sciences it is equivalent to.
claims: A habit covering principles and conclusion has the conclusion's subject as subject.
A single habit covering conclusions with different subjects has many subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2166.summary: Answers the fifth doubt: as already shown, there can be distinct sciences of the same subject because of different predicates.
claims: Distinct sciences of one subject arise from different predicates.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2173.summary: Objection: metaphysics considers being as being, another science considers it as subject of determinate properties, and these are not distinct properties but distinct modes of considering. So a different mode of considering alone causes diversity of sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2190.summary: Reply: what metaphysics and another science consider of being are distinct properties. Metaphysics shows properties of being (that is what considering it as being means), and another science its special properties. So the sciences with the same subject differ through different properties shown, and the mode of considering does nothing to differentiate them.
claims: Considering something 'as being' means demonstrating properties of being of it.
Different modes of consideration do not differentiate sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2221.summary: Proves this: a diverse mode of considering is either on the side of the object or only on the side of the intellect. If on the object's side, the object is only complex or incomplex, and a change of incomplex entails a change of complex, so there must be a different conclusion or premise. A different premise yields the same science (one conclusion proved by different principles is one science). A different conclusion with the same subject means a different property. If on the intellect's side, it could only be a difference of acts, but it seems impossible to have specifically distinct acts of knowing one and the same conclusion. So the distinction of sciences always requires distinction of subjects or predicates. Even those who say natural philosophy considers something as mobile and metaphysics as being mean only that one considers that it is mobile and the other that it is a being, which are distinct predicates. Science always concerns a complex, so the same subject alone yields no distinction. Averroes (De anima I, comm. 17) says metaphysics and natural science differ by considering different properties. So of the same subject there are several strict sciences only through diversity of properties.
claims: A mode of consideration on the object's side reduces to a difference of conclusions.
One conclusion proved by different principles belongs to one science.
There cannot be specifically distinct acts of knowing one conclusion.
Distinction of sciences always requires distinction of subjects or predicates.
Of one subject there are several sciences only through diverse properties.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2299.summary: Answers the first opinion's first argument: as shown, the subject does not first contain the predicate, nor knowledge of the subject knowledge of the predicate in the sense he explains, since distinct rationes cognoscendi are required on his own view. The predicate is sometimes more perfect than the subject. The subject also does not always contain knowledge of an immediate principle, since some immediate principles are not known from their terms.
claims: Some immediate principles are not known from their terms.
The predicate can be more perfect than the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2330.summary: Answers the second argument: the subject is not the adequate cause of the whole habit. Knowledge of the subject is a partial cause: for self-evident principles, knowledge of subject and of predicate are two partial causes, neither sufficient without the other. Against the inference that, being essentially rather than accidentally ordered, one must virtually contain the other: on the doctor's own principles, which Ockham accepts here, two partial causes can concur with neither receiving power from or being moved by the other, as he holds of intellect and object in intellection. So subject-knowledge and predicate-knowledge are partial causes, each with its own ratio, and the subject does not first contain, since it depends on the predicate as much as the reverse, sometimes more, and the predicate sometimes contains more perfectly. Strictly, in naturally discovered sciences it is the cognitions of subject and predicate that contain, on the view that universals have only objective being.
claims: Knowledge of the subject is only a partial cause of the scientific habit.
Two partial causes can concur without either containing the other.
Intellect and object are co-partial causes of intellection (Scotus, accepted).
Strictly, cognitions of terms contain, not the terms, on the objective-being view.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2398.summary: Answers the third argument: in essentially ordered things one stops at a first, but the first need not relate to the second as the second to the third. Object, intellection and volition are ordered, but volition is caused by and cannot exist without intellection, while abstractive intellection can exist without its object. Love can be more perfect than cognition though cognition is less perfect than its object. Matter is prior by nature to form and form to composite, yet form causes the composite and matter does not cause form. Form is more perfect than and causes its accident, while matter neither perfects nor causes form. So though knowledge of principles virtually contains knowledge of conclusions, knowledge of terms need not first contain knowledge of principles, nor one term another. Not every order is causal, especially efficient (genera and species are ordered without it). The subject can be first among knowables in some primacy, but not causal, so it need not contain the predicate. Not every first principle or immediate proposition is self-evident, and the predicate term is not known from the subject's ratio. The subject falls in the predicate's definition (taking definition broadly), but a definition depends on its other parts too, so knowledge of the subject is not sufficient.
claims: In an essential order, the first need not relate to the second as the second to the third.
Abstractive intellection can exist without its object.
Matter is prior by nature to form but does not cause it.
Not every order is causal.
Not every immediate proposition is self-evident.
The subject is only part of the predicate's definition, so knowing it is insufficient.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2513.summary: Turns to the main question, first setting out necessary distinctions. 'Subject' is taken either on the side of the object, as discussed and as the question intends, or as what the science informs, namely the soul, which is not what the question means.
claims: 'Subject of a science' may mean the subject of its conclusions or the soul in which it inheres.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2534.summary: Second distinction: the subject in the first sense can mean what supposits in the conclusion or, improperly, what it supposits for, and these differ. In 'every man is risible' the suppositing term is something common to all men, concept or not, while what it supposits for is singular. The proposition says only that every singular contained under 'man' can laugh, not that something common can. In 'every being is created or uncreated' the term is common to God and creatures but supposits only for singular beings. Sometimes they coincide, as in 'being is univocal to God and creature'.
claims: The subject term of a proposition differs from what it supposits for.
Common terms supposit for singulars in personal supposition.
In simple supposition the term supposits for itself, as in 'being is univocal'.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2576.summary: Third: hence the subject of a science differs from its object. The subject is the subject of the conclusion, while the object is what is known and terminates the act of knowing, namely the known conclusion. So the subject is part of the object, or only a partial object.
claims: The object of a science is the known conclusion; the subject is part of it.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2592.summary: Fourth: God, and any real being, can be understood in itself, so that nothing else terminates the act (as only whiteness terminates seeing). We cannot understand God that way in this life, never knowing God as particularly as this whiteness can be seen. Or God can be understood in something else, a concept, or on the other view a cognition common to God and others, wholly or in its parts. Then the concept must be proper to God, which can only be composite: we understand only 'the first, highest and infinite being' or the like. So something other than God terminates the act. It is not really God, though truly predicated of God, since it supposits not for itself but for God.
claims: In this life God cannot be understood in himself.
We understand God through a proper composite concept like 'first, highest, infinite being'.
The concept that terminates our act is not God but supposits for God.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2644.summary: On the opinion that concepts predicable of things for things are acts of understanding, God cannot be understood without something else being understood, by the whole act or its parts. Something can be understood either so that it alone is understood by an act (or an equivalent act), in which way God cannot be known by us under the common law, or by an act common in itself and its parts, proper neither simply nor equivalently, in which way God is understood by us by both simple and composite acts.
claims: On the intellectio theory, God cannot be understood by us without something else being understood.
God is understood in via by common acts, simple or composite.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2681.summary: Fifth distinction: science is sometimes numerically one and sometimes not, either because it covers diverse conclusions with the same subject (man is susceptible of learning, peccable, risible) or diverse conclusions with different subjects (animal, man, ass). Sixth: our theology possible in this state differs from theology possible to wayfarers by divine power. The latter may concern the same truths as ours, or truths in which God himself is subject or predicate, or a simple cognition proper to God.
claims: Science may be one numerically or many, with the same or different subjects.
By divine power wayfarers could have theology in which God himself is subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2718.summary: Transition: from these points and from the previous question, Ockham answers the form of the question.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2726.summary: First conclusion: taking 'subject' as what supposits, God under the ratio of deity is not the subject of our theology. The subject in this sense is a term of the conclusion, which immediately terminates the act of understanding or is that act. God in himself does not immediately terminate our act but only through a proper concept, and God is not a concept. So the concept, not God, is the subject of our theology.
claims: God under the ratio of deity is not the subject of our theology, taking subject as the suppositing term.
The concept proper to God is the subject of our theology.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2759.summary: Second conclusion: taking 'subject' as what is supposited for, God under the ratio of deity is the subject of some part of theology, the Father, Son or Holy Spirit of other parts, and creatures of yet others. In some truths the term supposits first for God ('God creates', 'God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit'), in others for the Father ('the Father generates', 'the Father is constituted by paternity'), and so for Son, Spirit and creatures. So diverse parts of theology have diverse subjects and theology has no single subject. This applies to strict science, faith and apprehensive habits, since complete theology possible in this life includes all of them.
claims: In terms of what is supposited for, God, the persons, and creatures are subjects of different parts of theology.
Theology has no single subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2801.summary: Third conclusion: the theology of the blessed, if about the same complexes as ours, has subjects proportionally like ours. But in their theology of truths where God himself, understood in himself and not just in a concept, is subject, God under the ratio of deity can be subject in both senses, since the term supposits for itself. For some truths the Father in himself is subject, and so on. The same holds for an intellect knowing the divine essence and persons abstractively in themselves.
claims: In the theology of the blessed, God under the ratio of deity can be subject in both senses.
The same holds for abstractive knowledge of the divine essence in itself.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2830.summary: On the opinion that predicables are acts of understanding, God is not the suppositing subject either in the blessed's theology or ours. In the blessed's theology a simple cognition proper to God alone is subject for some truths, and for others a common or composite cognition still proper to God. This applies to theology of contingent truths as well as necessary ones, since the subject of a known proposition is the subject of the science of it, whether known scientifically or not, and whether or not the predicate belongs first to it.
claims: On the intellectio theory, a cognition proper to God is the subject in theological propositions.
The analysis of subjects applies equally to contingent and necessary theology.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2865.summary: It follows that the subject of contingent truths is not always that to which the predicate first belongs, but the subject in that proposition, whether or not it belongs first. If it belongs first to another, those truths have distinct subjects.
claims: The subject of a contingent truth is the subject of the proposition, not necessarily the first bearer of the predicate.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2878.summary: Notes that almost all opinions on the subject of theology can in some way be verified by this account, though perhaps not as their holders meant.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2895.summary: The opinion that God under the ratio of deity is theology's subject can be verified by taking 'subject' as what is supposited for, and as first in some primacy. Among everything theological propositions supposit for, God is first by nature and causality relative to creatures and in some way prior relative to the persons. But God is not the first subject in the sense that knowledge of him virtually contains knowledge of all truths, nor of every part of theology, not of parts predicating things of the Father, Son, Spirit or creatures. The first subject of a cognition is what the predicate first belongs to and is subject in the known proposition, as the Father in 'the Father generates'.
claims: God is first among what theological propositions supposit for, by nature and causality.
God is not the first subject of every part of theology.
The Father is the first subject of 'the Father generates'.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2937.summary: The opinion that Christ is theology's subject can also be verified in a way: Christ is first among subjects in some primacy, containing divine and created nature, and so having unity with the divine persons and with creatures. But calling him the first subject is very improper.
claims: Christ can be called theology's subject only very improperly.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2955.summary: Likewise, it can be said that things and signs (res et signa) are theology's subject, since theology treats both: some things (God, creatures) and some signs (sacraments of the new and old law) are subjects. But not all things or all signs are subjects of our theology or of the blessed's.
claims: Some things and some signs, such as sacraments, are subjects of theology.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2971.summary: But the opinion that God is theology's subject under a ratio such as 'glorifier' seems wholly unreasonable: such rationes are predicates attributed to the subject ('God is glorifier, redeemer, restorer'), not the ratio of the subject.
claims: 'Glorifier', 'redeemer' and the like are predicates of theology, not rationes of its subject.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2989.summary: Raises a doubt: what theology is about, whether about everything or about some things and not others.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e2996.summary: Theology can mean the habit necessary for us in this state to attain eternal life (as in Augustine, De Trinitate XIV), or every theological habit whatever, necessary or not. In the second sense theology concerns all incomplexes but not all complexes. Every incomplex has some theological property predicable of it ('creatable', 'annihilable', 'perpetuable', 'separable from every other absolute thing', 'makeable without any secondary extrinsic cause'), and these properties are considered only in theology. As metaphysics, considering being, can show the properties of being of each thing contained under it, God, considered in theology, is the most common by causality, and theology's common properties belong to every effect. So in this sense theology concerns all incomplex things.
claims: Theology broadly taken concerns all incomplexes.
Every thing has theological properties such as 'creatable' and 'annihilable'.
Such properties are considered only in theology.
God is most common by causality, as being is by predication.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3071.summary: But not all complexes: many, such as 'every triangle has three angles...', are not theological at all, and theology concerns them only perhaps by predicating some theological property of them.
claims: Many complex truths, like geometrical theorems, are not theological.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3084.summary: In the first sense, our theology concerns neither all complexes nor all incomplexes, because the intellect barely suffices for what is necessary for salvation.
claims: Theology as necessary for salvation does not cover everything.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3093.summary: So in this state one should not, or need not, investigate other things, especially in particular.
claims: In this life one need not investigate what is unnecessary for salvation.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3100.summary: Answers the first principal argument: God is not the subject of every part of theology. One person is the subject of one part, another of another, and some creature of another, according to the properties considered.
claims: Different parts of theology have God, the persons, or creatures as subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3111.summary: Answers the second: Ockham concedes that something simply simple, if known in itself without any mediating object, is either wholly known or wholly unknown. But God cannot be so known by us, only through a mediating concept, which is the first object of that cognition, or through a cognition common to God and others. He denies that every subject can be known both distinctly and indistinctly. It suffices that the subject be known first without anything else, and that knowledge of something else about it be acquired later, which can happen with a simple thing.
claims: Something simply simple known in itself is known wholly or not at all.
God is known by us only through a mediating concept.
Not every subject must be knowable both distinctly and indistinctly.

wo8uy7-d1e166-d1e3137.summary: Answers the third: as shown in the first question, the same thing can be subject of a truth belonging to different sciences, because the same conclusion is reached from different principles, and the same subject can belong to different sciences through different properties. 'God is the first cause' belongs to metaphysics and theology, perhaps from different principles. Theology considers 'God is triune and creator', metaphysics 'God is good and wise'.
claims: The same truth can belong to different sciences through different principles.
'God is the first cause' belongs to both metaphysics and theology.

wo8uy7-d1e166.summary: Prologue question 9, annexed to the third principal question, asks whether God under the proper ratio of deity is the subject of theology. Most of the question criticizes Scotus's account of a science's first subject as what virtually contains all the science's truths. Ockham argues on empiricist grounds that incomplex knowledge of one thing never suffices for first knowledge of another. Abstractive knowledge presupposes intuitive knowledge caused by the thing itself, and an image only prompts recollection. Knowledge of a cause does not contain knowledge of its effect; connotative properties (beatifiable, creatable) import terms not contained in the subject; and even immediate propositions like 'heat is calefactive' require experience. He also deflates the notion of subject: it does not specify the science, give it dignity, or come first in knowledge. It is simply the subject of the known conclusion. Sciences of the same subject differ only through different predicates, not 'modes of consideration', and sciences like metaphysics have many ordered subjects rather than one, like kings of different kingdoms; being is first by predication, God by perfection. Applying this to theology, and distinguishing the suppositing term from what it supposits for, he concludes that God under the ratio of deity is not the subject of our theology, whose suppositing subject is a proper composite concept of God. As what is supposited for, God, the divine persons, and creatures are subjects of different parts, so theology has no single subject. In the theology of the blessed, God can be subject in both senses. He partially reconciles other opinions (God, Christ, res et signa), rejects 'God as glorifier', and holds that theology broadly concerns all incomplexes through properties like 'creatable', though theology necessary for salvation is narrower.
claims: The subject of a science does not virtually contain its truths.
Incomplex knowledge of one thing never suffices for first knowledge of another.
The subject of a science is just the subject of its known conclusions.
Sciences of one subject differ only through different predicates.
Our theology's suppositing subject is a concept proper to God, not God under the ratio of deity.
Theology has many subjects: God, the divine persons, and creatures.
Theology broadly concerns all incomplexes through theological properties.
